claim: Without a cue, only about 20 to 30 percent of people use a studied analogue on the radiation problem (about 10 percent with no source); a plain hint lifts the total to about 75 to 80 percent. The failure is access, not storage or mapping. Business-problem replications show a weaker and problem-dependent hint effect (factory 6.3 to 8.7 percent, HR 20.3 to 37 percent). Secondary restatements of Gick and Holyoak 1980 give 10 to 43 percent without a hint depending on the experiment (20 percent in Exp IV, 35 to 43 in Exp V); the primary text was still not opened in the gap search.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare: no cue, a failure-triggered cue at an impasse (stored solved subgoal surfaced), and an always-on cue; measure solve rate and tokens spent on cues.
audit_note: Gick & Holyoak 1983 (about 30% unhinted, about 75% with hint, 10% baseline; access gap) and Puranam & Sen (factory 6.3->8.7, HR 20.3->37) verified; in G&H 1983 Exp 4 the one-analog group reached only 53% total, so 75-80% is typical, not universal; the 1980 Exp IV/V figures at the end were not checked.

claim: Retrieval from memory is driven mostly by shared objects and surface content, not shared relational structure. Reminding rates: literal 0.56, surface 0.53, analogy 0.12, relations-only 0.09 (Exp 2). Surface and structure both matter for spontaneous transfer (Holyoak and Koh: 69 percent falling to 13 percent as both are removed). Models show the same pattern: GPT-4 does badly when a far analogy competes with a surface distractor (29.1 percent vs 50 random).
agent_test: Build a probe set where the useful stored case has no surface overlap and a decoy has high overlap; measure which one the agent retrieves with embedding lookup vs structure-aware lookup.
audit_note: GRF Exp 2 (.56/.53/.12/.09), Holyoak & Koh (69% to 13%) and ARN GPT-4 (29.1, random 50) verified; GRF Exp 3 shows object-only matches recalled just 17% vs 52% for objects plus first-order relations, so 'shared objects' alone is weaker than the wording suggests.

claim: People rate structural matches as the most sound inference sources while failing to retrieve them (soundness: analogy 4.40 vs surface 2.80; recall: analogy 0.44 vs surface 0.78 in Exp 1). Recognition after one week shows the structure was encoded (82 percent chose the literal match), so the gap is in access, not encoding.
agent_test: Show the agent a decoy and a structural match side by side and ask which to use (judgement) versus let it retrieve; the gap should favour judging over retrieving.

claim: Comparing two analogous cases and stating what they share improves later use of the principle: negotiation transfer 64 percent vs 23 percent (dyads, N=44), team replication 40 vs 22 percent (p=.06, marginal), consultants retrieved better own-memory cases (1.25 vs 0.82), meta-analytic d about 0.50 across 57 experiments (not re-opened by the cross-checker). Reading two cases without comparing does not help.
agent_test: When the agent solves problem B, force a written comparison with one stored solved case A and extract a shared schema; compare later solve rate on a third problem against storing A and B separately, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Thompson 64% vs 23% (N=44 dyads), Loewenstein 40% vs 22% (p=.06), Gentner 2009 1.25 vs 0.82, Alfieri d=0.50 over 57 experiments all verified; the first three are one research group, with only the Alfieri meta-analysis independent.

claim: Comparison done at retrieval time (comparing two probe examples, then searching memory) raises recall of the structurally similar earlier case (27 percent vs 6 percent, N=73) and cuts recall of the surface-similar one (30 vs 78 percent). A SME-built relational schema as the probe retrieves analogical matches (86 percent) where a single story probe returns shallow matches (86 to 100 percent). Same research group for the main data.
agent_test: On impasse, abstract the current problem into a relational description (or compare it to a second sibling problem) and use that as the memory query instead of the raw problem text.

claim: A two-stage retriever (cheap vector filter, then structural scoring of the few survivors) reproduces the human ordering of retrievability and runs about 100 times faster than the connectionist rival ARCS. Simulation: MAC passes about 3.3 items and FAC accepts 1.5. Rival LISA also claims a good fit to human reminding, and the speed comparison is by the MAC/FAC authors, so the model is not uniquely supported.
agent_test: Implement a cheap tag-count prefilter plus an LLM or structure-matching rerank of the top few; compare against embedding top-1 at equal retrieval cost.

claim: Embedding retrieval anchors on wording: when problems are paraphrased with structure kept, the correct item is usually in the top 10 but almost never first (hard tier Hit@1 0.0 percent; Hit@10 21.0 to 55.4 percent hard, 97.6 percent easy; in 95 to 99.8 percent of misses the winner is more lexically similar). Reasoning-heavy retrieval benchmarks show the same weakness (leading MTEB model 59.0 vs 18.3 on BRIGHT; BRIGHT was opened in the gap search: BM25 14.5 average, best retriever still below 30 even with GPT-4 reasoning queries).
agent_test: Measure Hit@1 and Hit@5 of the agent memory lookup on paraphrased versions of its own stored problems; report the gap between top-1 and top-10.
audit_note: Rashid & Kellis (Hit@1 0.0% hard; Hit@10 21.0/55.4 hard; 97.6 easy for Gemini, 95.2 for Qwen; 95.2-99.8% misses lexically closer) and BRIGHT (59.0 vs 18.3, BM25 14.5) verified; the 97.6% easy figure is for one embedder only and the Rashid paper is a single-author preprint.

claim: Retrieve-then-rerank closes part of the gap, but the gain depends on the judge and domain (5.4 to 63.3 percent of the recoverable gap in math; a naive lexical reranker hurts math). Adding structural sub-concepts to the query helps (retrieval 0.557 to 0.673 average) and LLM reranking gives the best top-1 pick. On BRIGHT, GPT-4 listwise reranking of BM25 results gave 14.3 to 17.4 at top-10 and 17.0 at top-100; a web-trained cross-encoder hurt (13.1 at top-10, 8.3 at top-100). Deeper reranking did not reliably pay.
agent_test: Top-10 by embedding, then ask the model to pick by shared structure; test whether the pick beats top-1, and report extra tokens used.
audit_note: Rashid (5.4-63.3% of gap closed, lexical control hurts math), Barakat & Kochmar (0.557->0.673) and BRIGHT Table 3 (BM25 14.3; GPT-4 17.4/17.0; MiniLM 13.1/8.3) verified; the 14.3 is the un-reranked BM25 baseline, and with the Google retriever GPT-4 depth 100 (22.6) did beat depth 10 (21.5), so 'not reliably' is right.

claim: Selecting exemplars by structure beats selecting by text embedding in few-shot maths (average exact match over 6 sets, BGE vs structure: 0.5B 27.6 vs 34.3; 1.5B 40.7 vs 47.1; 7B 66.2 vs 68.8; 72B 72.8 vs 74.4; math_qa slightly worse). Gains shrink with model size. Geometry proofs: analogical retrieval plus verifier lifts accuracy (o1 52 to 80, GPT-5 88 to 96 at the same 3x5 budget, N=50 problems) but that paper compares against no analogy, not against embeddings.
agent_test: Compare structure-keyed (operation graph, goal type, constraint type) vs embedding-keyed exemplar retrieval on held-out tasks with the same k and token budget.
audit_note: Table 2 of the graph-retrieval paper (BGE vs ours 27.6/34.3, 40.7/47.1, 66.2/68.8, 72.8/74.4; math_qa worse) and Sultan et al. (o1 52->80, GPT-5 88->96, 50 problems, 3x5 budget) verified; the PDF text extraction mislabels the table rows but the values match.

claim: Self-generated analogical prompting (recall K similar problems, then solve) gives small gains on easy maths (GSM8K GPT-3.5 77.8 vs 75.8 0-shot CoT and 76.7 5-shot; MATH 37.3 vs 33.9) and larger gains for code (Codeforces 9 to 13, 15 with knowledge). It beats retrieved labelled exemplars only for strong models. An independent test finds the gain is not tied to relevance. On five BIG-Bench Hard tasks, GPT-3.5 with self-generated relevant exemplars averaged 63.2, about 1.3 above none, so the effect is task-dependent.
agent_test: Run 0-shot, self-recall and fixed vetted exemplars on the agent task set at equal tokens; the cost of generating exemplars counts against it.

claim: Relevance of self-generated exemplars is not the driver: with GPT-3.5, relevant exemplars scored 71.5 GSM8K vs 75.5 with none and 75.1 to 76.3 with random ones; exemplar correctness matters (about 5 points lost with wrong answers) and a fixed vetted set (77.9) beats per-query generation and is cheaper. Llama-3.1-8B 81.0 vs 74.8; Qwen2.5-14B 91.1 vs 86.5. One paper only; its relevant-condition number is below the original paper 77.8, so prompt and setup differences may matter.
agent_test: Replace per-query self-generated analogues with a small vetted fixed bank; compare at equal tokens and check exemplar correctness separately from relevance.

claim: Adding self-generated high-level knowledge before exemplars helps on hard algorithmic tasks, because low-level exemplars alone cause copying of specifics (Codeforces GPT-3.5 13 to 15 percent; GPT-4 17 to 19; knowledge first beat exemplars first).
agent_test: On hard tasks, prompt for the general principle first, then the analogue, versus analogue only.

claim: Even with access solved, mapping and adaptation fail: a hint leaves success at about 75 percent in the radiation task and only 50 to 68 percent when the number correspondence is told (Novick and Holyoak 1991, seen only in a citing snippet). In LLM failure analysis, 28 of 50 failures had relevant, correct exemplars and the model still failed (12 generalisation gap, 8 over-reliance on an exemplar).
agent_test: After retrieval, add an explicit mapping step (what in A corresponds to what in B) and test with and without it at equal tokens.

claim: GPT-4 differs from people on access: with no hint it used the radiation analogue in 1 of 15 runs (but a surface-matching dolphin story in 14 of 15), with a hint recall 1.00 but precision about 0.50, and it used both stories when both were offered. Humans show high precision and low recall. GPT-3 on the original task found the convergence solution after the story (qualitative).
agent_test: Give the agent a mix of one structural and one surface-similar stored case and measure both recall and false-transfer rate with and without a hint.

claim: Agent memory systems that retrieve past trajectories by embedding similarity improve agents (ExpeL HotpotQA 28.0 to 39.0, ALFWorld 40 to 59; Memento +6.7 F1 average, best at K=4). The retrieval key matters inside a loop: ExpeL ALFWorld task-similarity key 59.0 vs reasoning-step key 48.5 vs random 42.5; InsightEmb (a trained key, 2026 preprint) turned text-similarity retrieval that was worse than no memory on WebShop (18.4 vs 31.0) into a gain (31.7). No paper compared a zero-training structural key with an embedding key at equal tokens inside the loop, and one paper argues retrieval is tuned to surface similarity rather than usefulness.
agent_test: In the agent loop, swap the memory key (embedding vs relational features) at equal K and tokens.

claim: Whether experts and ordinary people retrieve distant analogues from their own memory is contested: field studies found many far analogies, but a rival account says the generation task, not expertise, allows distant sources, and production studies still show a strong surface-similarity effect.
agent_test: Compare far-analogue yield of free generation versus cued retrieval from a stored bank on the same targets.

claim: Static diagrams or a verbal principle alone do not raise spontaneous access from one source (principle with one analogue: about 30 percent, no gain), but help when paired with two analogues (62 vs 40 percent) or when the diagram is animated (55 percent vs baseline-level static).
agent_test: Test whether adding a stated principle helps the agent only when two cases are shown.

claim: Cross-domain demonstrations can help a target domain if the model is above a size threshold, with gains from repaired reasoning structure rather than semantic cues (up to +12.3 percent ProofWriter to LogicalDeduction).
agent_test: Retrieve exemplars from a different task type with matching reasoning shape and compare with same-domain exemplars.

claim: Showing a model a structural match and a surface decoy side by side does not fix the failure. In 2023-era models the choice is already poor when the analogy is far and the decoy is near (GPT-4 29.1 percent vs 50 chance; humans 91.4), and decoys that keep the words but reverse the cause-effect order cut GPT-4 from 95.5 to 83.2 percent while humans stayed at 96 to 100, with 92 percent of GPT-4 errors being the decoy. The human split between good judgement and poor retrieval is therefore not the LLM pattern.
agent_test: Show the agent a retrieved case and a lexically close decoy together and require it to state the relation-by-relation mapping before use; count decoy picks with and without the mapping step.

claim: Loosened retrieval causes false transfer, and a polite 'ignore if it does not fit' instruction does not remove it. EconSkills: with no same-family skill, one approximate top-1 hint cut success 16.7 to 11.4 percent (p=.043); all 50 skills in context gave 11.4 percent vs 28.1 for no skill; five retrieved skills tied the baseline overall (28.3). InsightEmb: a progress-blind text-similarity key took WebShop from 31.0 to 18.4. A related preprint (abstract only) says self-graded memories inflate and compound the agent's own mistakes.
agent_test: Add an explicit no-match outcome to the lookup and a mapping check before use; compare solve rate on tasks with no true analogue in memory with and without the gate.

claim: Retrieving solved problems in the middle of reasoning helps small reasoning models at no extra token budget, mostly on hard items and weak models, and the gain falls as the base model gets stronger. ThinkRetrieve (309,609-item corpus, dense embeddings, retrieval at each stop-thinking boundary): AIME 2025 Qwen3-1.7B 24.4 to 35.6, Qwen3-4B 63.3 to 66.7, Qwen3-8B 67.8 to 71.1; GSM8K Qwen3-8B 96.1 to 97.2; retrieval at the start only gave no gain (88.80 vs 89.07); random per-step exemplars gave part of the gain.
agent_test: Inject one retrieved case at a mid-trace boundary vs at the start vs random, at equal total tokens, on items of varied difficulty.

claim: Trigger design is mostly untested for analogue retrieval. The only controlled trigger comparison found (FLARE, factual QA, 2023 models) shows confidence-gated retrieval matching always-on while retrieving for 40 to 80 percent of steps, and over-retrieval hurting on StrategyQA beyond 50 percent. A stagnation-gated controller for search agents cut search calls by 14 on average with +3 accuracy points (RAAC). No study compares a failure-triggered analogue cue with always-on retrieval in solve rate per token.
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: always-on retrieval, retrieval only after k steps without progress, and none.

claim: Reformulating the probe before search works without training, but the evidence is for answer-like or element-and-constraint rewrites, not for relational restating specifically. BRIGHT: LLM reasoning-step queries lifted retrieval by up to 12.2 points (BM25 14.5 average to about 27 with GPT-4). Buffer of Thoughts: a problem distiller before template lookup, with bigger drops when removed on hard tasks. ThinkRetrieve: query with the current intermediate answer 91.0 vs problem only 90.2. MetaLadder's restate step (+2.5 average) is only shown after fine-tuning. A short preprint warns extra reasoning can lower retrieval specificity.
agent_test: Compare lookup with the raw probe, a one-paragraph restatement, and a relation-tag abstraction of the probe, same memory, same K.
audit_note: Minor: BM25 14.5 to 27.0 is 12.5 points, slightly above the stated 12.2 headline; claim wording keeps both.

claim: Write-time abstraction of solved cases beats storing raw cases. AWM: abstract workflows beat retrieved concrete examples by +5.0 element accuracy and +4.0 step success on Mind2Web. EconSkills: a matched parameterised skill 49.3 vs 41.0 percent without; the raw matched trajectory 7.0 percent (confounded by length and format). ExpeL: insights from success-failure pairs need real experience and are worse with the agent's own reflections added. No study compares writing a schema from two cases against comparing the probe with a sibling at read time.
agent_test: Three memory arms at equal tokens: raw case, single-case abstraction, two-case schema; plus a read-time sibling comparison arm.

claim: Retrieval depth and memory size: a small rerank window is enough and a large dump of memory is harmful. BRIGHT: GPT-4 reranking top-10 17.4 vs top-100 17.0 on BM25 (21.5 vs 22.6 on a second retriever); EconSkills: all 50 skills in context 11.4 vs 28.1 percent for none. ThinkRetrieve keeps top-1 across 309,609 items and still gains. Rashid and Kellis rerank only top-10 so the top-10 vs top-50 question is still unmeasured on analogue retrieval.
agent_test: Grow the agent's memory from 50 to several thousand cases and plot top-1 solve rate with rerank depths 5, 10, 25 at fixed token cost.

claim: For strong base models, fixed exemplar prompts may stop helping. The DeepSeek-R1 report says few-shot prompting consistently degrades it (no numbers); ThinkRetrieve gains shrink from about +10 points for 1.7B models to +1 to 3 for 8B models on AIME and +0.8 on GSM8K. Analogical prompting beyond maths is small and task-dependent on GPT-3.5 (BBH +1.3). No test of analogical prompting on a current frontier model was found.
agent_test: Run on-demand retrieval vs fixed exemplars vs none on the agent's own base model across easy and hard items.

claim: Cheap prefilters that work in practice are abstract and coarse; nobody measured tag consistency. EconSkills retrieved using skill names and purposes only; Buffer of Thoughts used six coarse template classes plus an embedding threshold of 0.5 to 0.7; AWM replaced example-specific values with placeholders. None re-wrote the same case several times to check that tags agree across writes.
agent_test: Have the model tag the same stored case five times; report agreement of relation tags and the Hit@1 of tag-filtered lookup vs untagged.
